newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to deal with new Cambodia prime minister.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to deal with new Cambodia prime minister.

text.p: The United States on Thursday said it would deal with the newly-appointed first prime minister of Cambodia even though it considers the process of his selection undemocratic.

More than two-thirds of Cambodia's National Assembly members voted on Wednesday by secret ballot to accept Foreign Minster Ung Huot's nomination as first prime minister. He replaces Prince Norodom Ranariddh who was ousted in a July 6 coup by second prime minister Hun Sen.

"We'll be meeting with him in order to do business with the government of Cambodia ... But we do not believe that he was chosen democratically," State Department spokesman James Rubin told a news briefing.
He faulted the fact that the vote took place in the absence of many deputies and other parliamentarians who fled into exile during the coup. Ranariddh himself is in exile.
Rubin also said a constitutional question was raised because the assembly vice president was not there.
The U.S. assessment was not affected by King Norodom Sihanouk's statement that the country's acting head of state could appoint Ung Huot first prime minister, he said.

Rubin noted that Hun Sen had told U.S. envoy Stephen Solarz and a delegation from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations that Ranariddh's royalist party known as FUNCINPEC could present a new prime minister candidate if it chooses to do so.
Hence, "we are working closely with ASEAN and other friends of ... Cambodia to be sure that if they make another choice, that that choice would be accepted by Hun Sen," Rubin said.
"But we're trying to be sure that ASEAN takes the lead and that we're able to help ASEAN help FUNCINPEC make a choice that is democratic," he added.

After the coup, the United States suspended aid to Cambodia for 30 days while it assessed the situation and Hun Sen's pledge to comply with the 1991 Paris accords that ended Cambodia's civil war. That time period expires this weekend.
Rubin said "I wouldn't expect any significant changes in how we've approached it (aid), and that is that we will not provide funds to go through the government of Cambodia."

But Washington would continue humanitarian aid to Cambodia through non-governmental groups "to help the people of Cambodia ... who have suffered so under this regime and suffered far more greatly under the genocide of Pol Pot's (Khmer Rouge) regime," which killed more than one million people when it ruled Cambodia in 1975-79, he said.
